The Kestrel Valley Railway was chartered in the spring of 1874 by a consortium of quarry owners who had grown tired of hauling cut stone forty kilometres by cart to the nearest navigable river. The consortium was small — eleven men and one woman, the widow Harriet Ollen, who had inherited the largest of the quarries and, by most accounts, ran it better than her late husband ever had. Their charter allowed them to build a single-track line from the quarry heads at Barrow Ash down the valley floor to a junction with the main network at Denmoor, a distance the surveyors optimistically described as straightforward.

The first phase was indeed straightforward. The valley floor between Barrow Ash and the village of Little Wenn is almost flat, and the line was laid across it in nineteen months by a workforce that never exceeded four hundred men. Passenger services began in 1879, three years later than the charter had promised but early enough that the consortium's creditors stayed quiet. The original rolling stock consisted of two tank locomotives bought second-hand from a colliery in the north, six stone wagons, and a single passenger carriage that the company's own carpenter had built from the body of a horse-drawn omnibus.

The second phase was another matter entirely. Beyond Little Wenn the valley narrows and then closes altogether against the Hollowmere ridge, a mass of hard grey rock that stands between the upper valley and the plain at Denmoor. Three routes were surveyed. The first, a long detour to the south, would have added twenty-two kilometres and crossed land the company could not afford to buy. The second, a series of switchbacks up and over the ridge, was rejected as unworkable in winter. The third was a tunnel, and after two years of argument the tunnel was what the board chose. Work began at both portals in the summer of 1881 and continued, with two long interruptions caused by flooding, until the headings met in the autumn of 1886. The Hollowmere Tunnel, measured from portal to portal, is 4180 metres long, and for eleven years after it opened it was the longest railway tunnel in the region.

Money very nearly ended the project twice. In 1883 the company's treasurer, a man named Cabot Wrenn, was found to have moved a substantial sum into an account of his own; he left the country and was never prosecuted. The scandal cost the company its banking arrangements and forced a reorganisation in which the original consortium was diluted almost to nothing. Harriet Ollen kept her seat on the new board and held it until her death in 1901.

The reorganisation brought in a new chief engineer for the second phase. Ines Varga had trained on canal works abroad and had never built a railway tunnel before, which several members of the board mentioned frequently and loudly. She took charge in the winter of 1884, redesigned the ventilation shafts, replaced the contractor, and drove the remaining work to completion in under two years. Her report on the ventilation of long tunnels was reprinted three times and was still being cited by engineering schools forty years later.

The railway's profitable decades were shorter than anyone expected. Stone traffic peaked in 1911 and then fell away as concrete replaced cut stone in the cities the quarries had supplied. Passenger numbers held up until buses reached the valley in the 1930s, after which they collapsed. The line survived the war years carrying timber, limped through the 1950s on a subsidy, and closed to all traffic in 1963. The tunnel was sealed at both ends with brick.

A preservation society bought the section between Barrow Ash and Little Wenn in 1974, exactly one hundred years after the charter, and reopened it to visitors four years later. Today volunteers run trains on summer weekends, and the old goods shed at Barrow Ash holds a small museum: the carpenter's omnibus carriage, restored; a wall of photographs; and, in a glass case near the door, the theodolite that was used to set out the tunnel headings from both sides of the ridge.

Question: according to the passage, how long is the Hollowmere Tunnel in metres? Reply with only the number.

Read the following passage and then answer the question at the end.

The Halvern Coastal Station sits on a spit of shingle at the northern end of the Halvern Reserve, four hours by road from the nearest city and about ninety minutes on foot from the nearest paved surface. It was built in 1958 as a fisheries office, converted to a research station in 1971, and has been continuously occupied ever since, mostly by graduate students who arrive in September and leave, changed, the following June. The main building is a single storey of concrete and glass with a corridor down the middle and eleven rooms off it, of which four are laboratories, five are bedrooms, one is a kitchen that doubles as the only warm room in winter, and one contains the generator that everybody pretends not to hear.

The reserve itself covers just under three thousand hectares of dune, salt marsh and grazing meadow, bounded on the seaward side by the shingle spit and on the landward side by a drainage ditch that has been argued over by two parishes since the eighteenth century. Its ecological interest is out of all proportion to its size. The marsh supports a breeding population of wading birds that has been counted every spring since 1974, and the dune grassland behind it holds plant communities that exist nowhere else within two hundred kilometres. Grazing is managed with a small herd of hardy cattle, moved between compartments on a rotation that the station's staff revise every autumn after arguing about it for a week.

The reserve's most closely watched species is not a bird or a plant but an insect. The glass-winged moth is a small, unremarkable-looking creature whose larvae feed on a single species of dune sedge, and whose entire known range is the Halvern dune system and two smaller sites further along the coast. It is surveyed twice a year by light trapping along fixed transects, a method that has not changed since it was introduced in 1979 precisely so that the numbers stay comparable. In the most recent spring survey the population of glass-winged moths was counted at 3742 individuals, the highest figure recorded since 1991 and roughly double the low point of 2008, when a summer storm flooded the western compartments and destroyed most of the sedge.

Monitoring on this scale takes more electricity than a remote spit of shingle can easily provide. For thirty years the station ran on diesel, trucked in by the barrel along the beach at low tide. That ended in 2016, when the trust that owns the reserve installed a tidal turbine in the channel two hundred metres offshore. The turbine, named Marisol after the trust's founder, is rated at 240 kilowatts, which is far more than the station consumes; the surplus is exported and the income pays for roughly a third of the station's running costs. Diesel is still kept on site, in two tanks behind the generator room, for the four or five days a year when the turbine is shut down for maintenance.

The station's staff consists of a warden, an assistant warden, a part-time bookkeeper who visits on Thursdays, and between two and six researchers depending on the season. Volunteers come for a week at a time, mostly in summer, and are put to work on fence repair, sedge counts, and the endless business of removing sea buckthorn from places where it is not wanted. The warden since 2019 has been Peter Onnela, who arrived as a volunteer in 2004, left to work elsewhere for a decade, and came back.

Visitors are welcome, within limits. There is a hide at the southern end of the marsh, reachable by a boardwalk, and a path along the landward edge of the dunes that is open all year except during the breeding season, when a stretch of about eight hundred metres is closed. The station itself is not open to the public, except on one Saturday each September, when the staff put out signs, brew an alarming quantity of coffee, and let anyone who has walked the ninety minutes from the road look through a microscope at a sedge leaf.

Question: according to the passage, how many glass-winged moths were counted in the most recent spring survey? Reply with only the number.
